title.rendered: D-2 vocational program visa changes: who qualifies, required documents and the stepwise application route

content.rendered:
Overview

D-2 vocational program visa changes (D-2 is the student visa category for degree and vocational training) have adjusted accreditation and practical training permissions for some vocational institutions in Korea.

This shift follows Ministry of Justice and HiKorea updates and may affect admission conditionality, on-campus and off-campus practicum allowances; this article clarifies who is affected and the procedural steps to apply or adjust status.

Visa purpose

The updated D-2 track is intended to permit enrolled international students to complete vocational curricula along with supervised practical training when the host institution holds approved vocational accreditation.

The visa aims to align academic and industry training while maintaining immigration control through accredited program lists and specific work-permission conditions.

Eligibility

Eligibility now depends on both the applicant’s acceptance by an accredited vocational program and the program’s explicit approval for practical training components by the immigration authority.

Key eligibility points to confirm before application include program accreditation status, financial sufficiency, and whether the planned practical training is classified as curricular (credit-bearing) or extracurricular (non-credit); applicants moving from study to employment may consider pathways such as E-7 Work if they meet professional sponsorship criteria.

  • Program accreditation: Confirm the institution is on the immigration-approved vocational list before applying.
  • Admission letter: Obtain an official letter that specifies practical training components and expected hours.
  • Financial stability: Show funds to cover tuition and living costs for the term stated in the acceptance.
  • Immigration history: Maintain a record free of disqualifying violations that could block approval.

Documents

The document set for the updated D-2 application includes standard student visa evidence plus program-specific confirmations of vocational accreditation and the practical training schedule.

Applicants should prepare certified copies and translations where necessary and follow document templates specified by immigration to avoid processing delays; additional institutional letters supporting practicum placements are frequently requested and can be verified via the university.

  • Admission letter: Original or certified copy naming the vocational program and practicum details.
  • Proof of accreditation: Document from the institution or a government list confirming the program’s vocational approval.
  • Financial evidence: Bank statements, scholarship letters, or sponsor declarations covering tuition and living costs.
  • Passport and photos: Valid passport and passport-format photos meeting HiKorea specifications.
  • Criminal record or health checks: If requested by the issuing office, supply originals or certified translations.
  • Practical training agreement: A signed agreement for on-site training when practicum is part of the curriculum.

Application steps

Submit the visa application to the Korean diplomatic mission in your country or apply for status change/extension through the HiKorea portal (online immigration service) when already in Korea.

Follow the institution’s guidance for issuing an electronic Confirmation of Visa Issuance (if applicable), upload accredited program evidence, and track the application through the official channels; domestic applicants should also review Extension procedures if converting status.

  1. Pre-check: Confirm the vocational program appears on the immigration-approved list and collect institutional confirmations.
  2. Document assembly: Prepare certified copies, translations, and a practicum agreement as required.
  3. Consular or online filing: File the visa application at the Korean embassy/consulate or via HiKorea for status adjustments.
  4. Biometrics and interview: Attend any scheduled biometrics appointment or consular interview and respond to requests for clarification.
  5. Decision and entry: Receive the visa or status change notice and follow entry or registration steps listed by the issuing office and the host university.

Fees and processing

Application fees and processing expectations vary by filing location and whether the case is an initial visa issuance or a domestic status change; applicants should not assume identical timings between consular offices and HiKorea online service.

Typical consular fees, administrative surcharges, and optional courier costs may apply and institutions sometimes charge service fees for issuing required accreditation letters; consult the issuing mission or university for precise amounts before payment.

Aspect Previous practice Updated practice
Program evidence General admission letter often sufficient Formal accreditation proof and practicum agreement required
Work permissions during study Limited standard part-time allowances Practicum classified and approved by institution may allow curricular practicum hours
Processing channel Mostly consular-based issuance Greater use of HiKorea online procedures for status adjustments

Rejection or change scenarios

Applications may be refused if program accreditation is missing, the practicum agreement is inadequate, or the applicant cannot demonstrate required financial or background checks.

If a refusal or a need to change status occurs, applicants should obtain a written decision, address cited deficiencies, and reapply or request an administrative review through the Ministry of Justice channels; consideration of alternative visas such as sponsored employment paths should follow only after confirming eligibility.

  • Missing accreditation: Obtain official confirmation from the university and resubmit with the accreditation document.
  • Insufficient practicum details: Secure a signed practicum agreement that specifies hours, supervision, and learning outcomes.
  • Status change denied: File a corrective application using HiKorea guidance or consult the institution’s international office for support.

Official source and checked date

This guidance is based on procedural information and notices published by the Ministry of Justice of the Republic of Korea and the HiKorea immigration portal, which govern visa eligibility and status procedures.

Readers should verify specifics at the Ministry of Justice (MOJ) and HiKorea (HiKorea) and note that the referenced immigration procedures were checked on 2026-09-12 for current accuracy; students should also consult their admitting institution such as those listed at Study in Korea for program-level confirmation.

Photo: Marta Branco / Pexels (License) · Stock photo / 자료사진

자주 묻는 질문 (FAQ)

Can I work during a D-2 vocational program if my practicum is unpaid?

You must check whether the practicum is classified as curricular and approved by the institution; curricular practicum approved by immigration may be permitted while extracurricular unpaid placements often do not change standard part-time work restrictions.

Where do I submit proof of vocational accreditation for my D-2 application?

Submit accreditation proof with your visa application at the consulate or upload it via the HiKorea online portal for domestic status adjustments, and keep originals for verification by the issuing authority.

What happens if my university loses vocational accreditation after I enter Korea?

Notify immigration and your international office immediately; you may be required to change status, transfer to an accredited program, or apply for a different visa depending on the remedial options allowed by MOJ.

Is an employer sponsorship possible after completing a D-2 vocational track?

Employer sponsorship is possible if you meet the criteria for work visas such as E-7, including occupational fit and salary requirements, and you should plan transitions in coordination with prospective employers and immigration guidance.

Who should I contact for procedural help with D-2 visa issues?

Contact your university international office first for program documentation and then consult the nearest Korean embassy/consulate or the HiKorea portal for immigration-specific procedural assistance.

title.rendered: E-7-T Top-Tier jobseeker visa: who qualifies, required documents, application steps and next actions

content.rendered:
The E-7-T Top-Tier jobseeker visa permits high-skilled foreign professionals to enter Korea to seek employment in designated priority industries. This guide explains the visa purpose, eligibility criteria, document checklist, application steps, fees and possible outcomes based on official sources.

Purpose and permitted activities

The E-7-T visa is designed to attract highly qualified candidates for sectors where Korea has recognized shortages of specific professional skills. Holders may enter to pursue direct employment offers or employer recruitment processes and must comply with work conditions set by the immigration permit.

Who can apply and basic qualifying criteria

Eligibility requires evidence of high-level qualifications, such as advanced degrees, specialized professional experience, or industry-recognized achievements that match designated occupational fields. Applicants must also meet nationality, criminal record, and health screening standards specified by immigration authorities.

  • Educational background: Advanced university degree or equivalent professional certification in a relevant field.
  • Work experience: Documented professional experience in the targeted sector when required by the occupation list.
  • Recruitment status: Either a confirmed employer recruitment pathway or documented job-seeking plan in priority industries.
  • Legal background: Clean criminal record certificates and required medical checks.

Required documents and format guidance

Applicants must prepare certified originals or notarized copies for each principal document and provide translations into Korean when documents are not in Korean or English. Typical items include passports, academic diplomas, employment records, a resume or CV, sealed criminal record checks, medical examination results, and any employer letters or recruitment notices.

  • Passport: Valid passport with at least one blank visa page.
  • Degree certificates: Apostilled or consular-certified diplomas and transcripts with Korean or English translations.
  • Employment records: Letters of reference, contracts, or employer recruitment confirmations showing role and salary scale.
  • Criminal record check: National police certificate from country of residence and any prolonged stays, translated and certified.
  • Medical report: Health examination covering communicable diseases as required by immigration rules.

How to apply: step-by-step process

Most applicants submit a pre-approval or visa application through the HiKorea online portal (the immigration service system) and follow instructions for document upload and appointment scheduling. After approval, applicants complete consular visa processing if outside Korea, or apply for a change of status at the local immigration office if already in-country.

  1. Prepare certified documents and translations as listed above.
  2. Register and file the application through the HiKorea portal or with the sponsoring employer’s application channel.
  3. Attend interviews or provide additional evidence if requested by immigration officers.
  4. Receive approval notice, then obtain the visa at a Korean consulate or change status in Korea and register residency as required.

Fees, processing considerations and visa validity

Application fees and processing timelines vary by consulate location and by whether an applicant is applying from abroad or seeking a change of status inside Korea. Processing can be delayed by incomplete documentation or requests for additional verification, and applicants should consult HiKorea for case-specific timeframes and fee schedules.

Feature E-7-T (Top-Tier) Comparison: D-10 (Job Seeker) Comparison: E-7 (General Work)
Primary purpose Targeted entry for high-skilled recruitment or job search in priority sectors General job-seeking and vocational search activities Employment under employer sponsorship for specified occupations
Typical documentation Advanced qualifications, employer recruitment evidence, certified diplomas Proof of intent to seek work, qualifications moderate Employment contract and employer sponsorship documents
Change of status Allowed with employer sponsorship and required paperwork Can convert to work visa if employment is secured Primary intended use; change possible between employers with notification

Refusal, extension, and change of circumstance procedures

Common reasons for refusal include insufficient evidence of the claimed qualifications, mismatches between the applicant’s profile and the designated occupation list, or incomplete certification and translation of documents. Applicants who are refused may submit additional evidence, appeal administrative decisions, or reapply after addressing the cited deficiencies, and changes of employer or job category require formal notification and approval by immigration.

  • Refusal reasons: Missing notarizations, unverifiable employment claims, or inadmissibility issues.
  • Remedies: Provide certified replacements, request consular guidance, or pursue administrative appeal within prescribed deadlines.
  • Extensions and changes: File extension or change-of-status applications prior to permit expiry and submit updated contracts or sponsor letters.

Further checks and official guidance sources

Applicants must confirm case-specific requirements and up-to-date procedures directly with official channels before submitting applications to avoid processing delays. The Ministry of Justice immigration pages and the HiKorea portal are the authoritative sources for directives, forms, and recent procedural notices, and these pages were checked on 2026-09-12 for current procedural guidance.

  • Ministry of Justice (immigration guidance)
  • HiKorea (online immigration portal)

If you are comparing study and entry options before applying, consider how the E-7-T differs from student or cultural routes and consult relevant guidance on related visas. See the D-2 Student page for student-to-employment pathways, the Working Holiday overview for short-term work options, and the Study in Korea portal for education-related transitions, or browse our main Visa Guide index for broader comparisons.

자주 묻는 질문 (FAQ)

What minimum documents are required to apply for E-7-T?

Primary documents include a valid passport, apostilled or certified degrees with translations, employment records or recruitment confirmation, criminal record check, and a health examination as required by immigration.

Can I change employer after receiving the E-7-T permit?

Any change of employer or job category requires immigration notification and approval; you must submit new contracts and sponsor documents before starting the new role.

Where should I submit the application if I am outside Korea?

Apply through the HiKorea portal for pre-approval and then submit required visa paperwork to the Korean consulate or embassy responsible for your place of residence.

How long do processing times typically take?

Processing times vary by consulate and case complexity; consult the HiKorea portal and the Ministry of Justice pages for current estimates and case-specific notices.

What steps follow if the visa application is refused?

Review the refusal notice, provide certified supplemental evidence if applicable, consider administrative appeal options, or correct deficiencies and reapply.

title.rendered: Applying for Korea F-1-D workation: required documents and application steps

content.rendered:
Purpose and immediate context

Many foreign residents preparing to work temporarily from Korea must assemble F-1-D workation visa documents to show permission for short-term remote work activities while in the country. The Ministry of Justice and HiKorea set documentary standards that immigration officers use at visa application and entry checks, and this piece explains the main evidence types, how to apply and what to do if a submission is incomplete or refused.

Who may qualify and basic eligibility

Eligibility typically requires proof of lawful residence outside Korea, an employment relationship or contractual arrangement permitting remote work, and a clear purpose and period of stay that match the workation intent. Immigration may also check whether the applicant will use local services or enter local labor markets that would require a different visa category such as E-7 Work or a student permit like D-2 Student status when responsibilities go beyond remote activities.

Main documents required

Applicants must provide identity and travel documents plus written evidence that ties the remote work to an employer or client, and authorities may ask for originals or certified copies during processing. The list below describes common items requested by immigration and consular offices, but officials may request additional evidence depending on nationality and individual circumstances.

Document Why it is requested Original / Certification
Passport Establishes identity, nationality and validity for travel and visa stamp. Original required at submission.
Visa application form and photo Standard consular processing items to register the application. Completed form and recent photo supplied; originals on request.
Letter from employer or client Confirms remote work, role, contract period and that work will be done remotely rather than in local employment. Signed original or company letterhead; notarisation may be requested.
Employment contract or freelance agreement Shows remuneration, duties and period of engagement relevant to stay length. Certified copy is often sufficient, original if asked.
Proof of funds and travel itinerary Demonstrates ability to support stay and return travel plans without local employment. Bank statements and booking confirmations; originals not usually required but may be checked.
Health insurance Shows coverage for medical costs while in Korea to reduce public burden. Policy certificate copy; original if requested.
Criminal record check Used to confirm admissibility where serious convictions may bar entry. Certified translation and apostille or consular legalisation may be required.

Preparing and submitting the application

Start by assembling the items in the table and securing any notarisation or translation before submission to the Korean embassy or consulate that handles your nationality, unless your embassy directs you to complete processes through the HiKorea system. Applicants should follow the consulate checklist and consider contacting the visa section in advance to confirm whether documents can be uploaded online or must be presented in person, and those who enter Korea with an appropriate entry stamp should check local registration requirements.

Step-by-step actions applicants commonly follow

  • Prepare: Collect passport, photos, employer letter, contract, proof of funds and insurance.
  • Certify: Obtain notarisation, apostille, or official translations if requested by the consulate.
  • Submit: File the application with the embassy/consulate or as directed by HiKorea and pay any required fee.
  • Attend: Attend an interview or provide biometrics if the consulate requests them.
  • Register: Upon arrival, comply with any alien registration or notification rules and, if needed, use the Extension process for longer stays.

Fees, typical processing considerations and timing

Visa fees and processing times differ by applicant nationality and by whether the application is handled at a consulate, in the HiKorea online channel or at a point of entry, so applicants must confirm the fee schedule at the relevant embassy or on HiKorea. Processing can also be affected by requests for additional documents or background checks, and applicants should allow extra time for certification, translations and postal services when preparing filings.

If the application is refused or you need to change status

Common reasons for refusal include inadequate proof of remote-only work, missing certifications, or evidence that the proposed activity requires a different visa category, and officials will provide a refusal notice indicating the main grounds. Where a different status is appropriate candidates should consider switching to a student route for academic study or to a sponsored work visa and seek further guidance on options such as D-2 Student or E-7 Work procedures, and jobseekers may consult local listings such as the Jobs portal for employment sponsorship options.

Official references and last verification

The procedural expectations in this article are based on guidance from the Korean Ministry of Justice and the HiKorea immigration portal, which publish visa categories, application channels and documentary requirements. Official pages were checked on 2026-06-01 and readers must confirm current rules at the Ministry of Justice (https://www.moj.go.kr/moj/index.do) and HiKorea (https://www.hikorea.go.kr) before submitting any application.

자주 묻는 질문 (FAQ)

What is the quickest way to confirm required documents for my nationality?

Contact the Korean embassy or consulate responsible for your country and cross-check with the HiKorea portal, as requirements can vary by nationality and are updated by the Ministry of Justice.

Can an employer letter be digital or must it be a notarised paper document?

Many consulates accept scanned letters for the initial review but may require an original or notarisation for final processing, so secure certification in advance where possible.

If my visa is refused, can I appeal the decision inside Korea?

The refusal notice will indicate appeal or reapplication options and applicants facing refusal should consult the Ministry of Justice guidance or seek consular instructions about administrative review or reapplication.

title.rendered: How a Conviction as an 암살자 (violent crime) Impacts Korean Visa Eligibility, Applications and Remedies

content.rendered:
Immediate finding, context and article scope

A criminal conviction for violent acts described as 암살자 (assassin) is treated as a serious disqualifier under Korea’s immigration screening for entry and long-term stay. This page outlines how such a conviction is assessed, which visa pathways are most affected, the documents officials require, the stepwise application and reporting process, likely fees and processing time, and options after refusal or revocation.

Purpose and relevance to visa decisions

Korean immigration policy evaluates public safety and good conduct as core purposes when granting visas and residency. The Ministry of Justice and HiKorea both use criminal-history information to determine whether admission or continued stay threatens public order and safety.

Who is affected and basic eligibility constraints

Applicants with convictions for severe violent crimes face higher risk of denial for short-stay and long-stay visas alike, and may be subject to entry bans or deportation orders. Eligibility can differ by visa class and individual circumstances such as sentence completion, rehabilitation evidence, and whether the conviction is foreign or domestic.

Core documents immigration will request

Authorities will typically require an authenticated criminal record certificate from the country of conviction and a certified Korean translation; fingerprint or biometric data may be required during interview or entry processing. Additional supporting documents include judicial judgments, certificates of rehabilitation or pardon, and any probation or parole completion papers.

  • Criminal record certificate: full national police or court-issued record from the convicting country with apostille or consular legalization where required.
  • Judgment and sentencing documents: court rulings showing offense details, sentence length, and completion or ongoing status.
  • Rehabilitation evidence: certificates, employer reference letters, or treatment program completion that speak to rehabilitation.
  • Translations and authentications: Korean translations certified according to HiKorea guidance.

How to apply and what steps to expect

Submit the usual visa application package to the Korean embassy or consulate abroad or file online at HiKorea where permitted, and include full criminal-history documentation as required by the consular checklist. Expect a supplemental review step by immigration officers that can include interviews, additional document requests, or biometric verification to assess risk to public safety.

  • Initial submission: follow embassy or HiKorea application procedures with certified documents.
  • Supplemental review: immigration may request more records or an in-person interview during visa processing.
  • Final decision: visa grant, refusal, conditional admission, or request for withdrawal may follow based on risk assessment.

Fees, processing timelines and administrative notes

Visa application fees and processing timelines follow the standard fee schedule for the visa category applied, and additional costs may arise from document authentication and translation. Processing time for cases involving serious criminal records is usually longer because of inter-agency checks and possible requests to foreign authorities for confirmation.

Visa category Effect of violent conviction Typical additional checks
Short-term tourist / visit High likelihood of refusal if conviction is recent or sentence incomplete Police certificate and entry ban database check
Working Holiday Likely refusal when convictions involve intentional serious harm Background check and consular interview; see Working Holiday guidance
E-7 Work Employers and immigration screen stringently; serious convictions often bar issuance Employer checks, criminal record, and possible job suitability review
Long-term residency / family visas High scrutiny with stronger grounds for refusal or revocation Detailed judicial documents and rehabilitation proof required

When visas are refused, revoked, or must change

A visa can be refused at initial application or revoked after issuance if new information about a violent conviction emerges or if the holder fails to disclose convictions. Remedies may include administrative appeal, submission of fresh rehabilitation evidence, or reapplication after legally required waiting periods when applicable.

  • Refusal: consular or immigration decision to deny entry or visa issuance based on risk assessment.
  • Revocation: cancellation of an already-issued visa following discovery of undisclosed convictions or breach of conditions.
  • Appeal and mitigation: follow the appeal procedures set by the issuing office and provide compelling rehabilitation documentation.

Special notes for specific pathways and employers

Work visas such as E-7 usually involve employer sponsorship and can be more sensitive to serious criminal history because employers bear compliance risk for foreign workers. Applicants should consult prospective employers and the hiring process on Jobs listings and verify company willingness to support background-review requests when relevant.

Applicants seeking non-work pathways, including Working Holiday options or extensions, should review the policy carefully because short-term schemes can still be denied for public-safety reasons. For visa holders already in Korea needing extra stay time, see procedural guidance on Extension and for work sponsorship and category-specific rules consult the E-7 references on this site.

Practical compliance checklist before applying

Obtain an authenticated full criminal record and certified translation, and disclose convictions proactively on application forms to avoid administrative penalties for nondisclosure. Prepare supporting rehabilitation documentation and, if applying for employment-based visas, obtain employer confirmation that they will proceed with hiring and paperwork.

  • Authenticate records: apostille or consular legalization as required by the issuing country and Korea.
  • Translate: certified Korean translations following HiKorea instructions.
  • Employer support: letter of intent or contract for work visas such as E-7 Work.
  • Job search resource: verify openings and employer policies on background checks at Jobs.

Where to confirm rules and how current guidance was checked

Main program rules and legal bases are published by the Ministry of Justice and by HiKorea, which administers visa applications and immigration services; applicants should consult those sources for case-specific protocols. This article references procedures and document requirements consistent with the Ministry of Justice (https://www.moj.go.kr/moj/index.do) and HiKorea (https://www.hikorea.go.kr) and was checked against those sources on 2026.

자주 묻는 질문 (FAQ)

Can a past conviction for violent crime automatically ban me from all Korean visas?

Not automatically; serious violent convictions create strong grounds for refusal but each case is individually assessed by immigration considering sentence completion and rehabilitation evidence.

Do I need to submit a criminal record if my conviction was in a foreign country?

Yes; you must submit an authenticated criminal record from the country of conviction along with certified Korean translations when requested by the embassy or HiKorea.

Is there a route to appeal a visa refusal based on criminal history?

Yes; consular and immigration decisions may be appealed or re-challenged with new evidence of rehabilitation, legal certificates, or a pardon where applicable.

Will an employer accept applicants with a serious conviction for visa sponsorship?

Employers often perform their own checks and many will decline to sponsor applicants with severe violent convictions, but employer willingness varies by industry and company policy.

Where can I find the official instructions for document authentication and translation?

Follow the guidance on HiKorea for document submission rules and the Ministry of Justice site for legal bases and procedural notices.

title.rendered: Practical steps to qualify for and apply for Korea long-term F-2 visa residency

content.rendered:
Why applicants choose this long-term residence status

Korea long-term F-2 visa is a residency category used by foreigners who seek extended stay without immediate permanent residency. The status supports family life, work permission under conditions, and longer-term stability (HiKorea).

Who typically qualifies and key criteria

Eligibility usually follows two principal routes: family/marriage connections and a points-based qualification for skilled residents. Basic criteria include verified identity, stable income or support, and compliance with immigration rules (Ministry of Justice).

Core documents to prepare

Applicants must collect primary identification, proof of legal stay or relationship in Korea, and evidence of financial means or points documentation. Typical sets include passport, valid Alien Registration or visa copy, application form, and supporting certificates from employers or family (HiKorea).

Step-by-step application process

Apply at a local immigration office in Korea or through the HiKorea online portal, following document submission and fee payment steps. Expect administrative review, possible interview, and notification by post or electronic message (HiKorea).

Costs, timing and what to expect

Fees include the application charge and any document translation or notarisation costs, which vary by office and service provider. Processing commonly completes within several weeks but can extend depending on document complexity and workload at the immigration office (Ministry of Justice).

When applications are refused or status must change

Refusal reasons typically include insufficient evidence, criminal records, or unmet points criteria for the points-based route. Applicants can submit additional documents, file an administrative appeal, or convert status where permitted under immigration rules (Ministry of Justice).

Comparing common F-2 routes

Route Typical validity Key requirement Documents emphasised
Family / marriage-based One to multiple years, renewable Proven family or marriage relationship Marriage certificate, family registry, cohabitation proof
Points-based (long-term residency) One to multiple years, renewable Demonstrated points score and stability Employment records, income proofs, qualifications

Related pathways and internal resources

Applicants with work offers should also review employer-based permits such as the E-7 Work visa for comparative rules. Students and working holiday entrants should check D-2 Student and Working Holiday rules and the Study in Korea guidance for transition options.

Practical checklist before you submit

  • 1: Valid passport with spare validity beyond requested permit period.
  • 2: Completed application form and passport photo.
  • 3: Proof of relationship or points evidence.
  • 4: Financial or employment proof and any translations.
  • 5: Payment for application fee and processing receipts.

Primary official references and verification date

Official guidance and forms are available from HiKorea and the Ministry of Justice, which govern eligibility and processing rules (HiKorea). Sources checked on 2026 for current procedural requirements and local office contacts (Ministry of Justice).

자주 묻는 질문 (FAQ)

What is the main purpose of this residency status?

The status provides longer-term residence for family, marriage, or qualified skilled residents, enabling stability and conditional work permission.

Where do I submit the application?

Submit at a local immigration office in Korea or via the HiKorea online portal following the document checklist and fee payment.

How long does processing usually take?

Processing commonly takes several weeks but can be longer depending on document complexity and office workload.

Can a student change from D-2 to this status?

Converting from D-2 Student to this residency is possible where eligibility is met and supporting documents are supplied.

title.rendered: How to Complete HiKorea Online Employment Reporting for Foreign Work and Study Visas in Korea

content.rendered:
Visa purpose

HiKorea online employment reporting is the official channel to notify Korean immigration when a foreign national starts, changes, or ends employment that affects their visa conditions. The reporting requirement exists to keep a migrant’s residence record accurate and to show compliance with the Immigration Control Act as administered by the Ministry of Justice and HiKorea.

Eligibility

Reporting obligations typically apply to holders of work-related and study visas when employment affects their residency status or conditions attached to their visa. Common visa types that often require reporting include D-2 Student and E-7 Work, but the exact obligation depends on the specific visa subtype and the terms granted by immigration.

  • Primary visa holder: The foreign national whose status is affected must ensure the report is made, either personally or with employer assistance.
  • Employer notification: Employers are commonly expected to cooperate and supply documents when the report concerns change of employer or job role.
  • Representative filing: Authorized representatives can file online on HiKorea if the foreign national grants permission or provides required identification data.

Documents

The basic document set for most online employment reports includes identification, employment contract or employer confirmation, and a copy of the passport or alien registration details. Additional supporting documents may be requested by immigration based on the visa type, the nature of employment, or if the record requires verification.

Situation Typical documents Where to upload
New employment Employment contract or official offer letter; passport/ARC data; employer registration details HiKorea online portal document upload section
Change of employer New contract, termination letter from prior employer, employer confirmation HiKorea online change report form

title.rendered: Korean Visas and Immigration: Know the Cost and Eligibility

content.rendered:
Korean visa eligibility depends mainly on your purpose of stay, nationality, intended length of residence, and supporting documents. Costs also vary by visa type, nationality, application location, and extra services, so check the responsible Korean embassy, consulate, or official immigration portal before paying.

Start with the purpose of your stay

The correct visa is usually determined by what you will do in Korea, not simply by how long you want to remain. Common categories include:

  • Short visits: tourism, business meetings, family visits, or other temporary activities. Some nationalities may qualify for visa-free entry or a separate electronic travel authorization, but those options are not the same as a visa.
  • Study and training: university study, language programs, and certain vocational or research activities generally use different student or trainee classifications.
  • Employment: work visas are tied to the role, employer, qualifications, and sometimes professional licensing or sponsorship requirements.
  • Family and residence: dependent, marriage, long-term residence, and permanent residence categories each have their own relationship, income, residence, and conduct requirements.

Do not choose a category only because it appears to offer a longer stay. Activities allowed under one status may be prohibited under another, and changing status inside Korea may be restricted.

What Korean visa costs usually include

The headline visa fee is only one possible expense. Build a full application budget around these items:

  • Visa issuance or examination fee, which may differ by nationality, entry type, and validity.
  • Application-centre, courier, payment, or appointment charges where those services are used.
  • Document preparation, including certified translations, notarisation, apostilles, legalisation, photographs, and bank-document fees.
  • Costs connected with residence registration, an alien registration card, extensions, status changes, or reissuance after arrival, where applicable.
  • Travel, accommodation, and employer or school paperwork costs if an appointment or original-document submission is required.

Ask the embassy or consulate for the fee schedule that applies to your nationality and place of application. A fee paid for processing is generally not a guarantee of approval, and additional requests can create further costs.

Eligibility: the evidence officers examine

Although requirements differ by category, a credible application normally connects four points: your stated purpose, your qualifications, your finances, and your plans after entry. Officers may assess:

  • Whether the proposed activity matches the selected visa category.
  • Whether you have the required passport validity and prior immigration history.
  • Whether your funds, sponsorship, accommodation, or employment documents support the planned stay.
  • Whether a Korean school, employer, family member, or other sponsor must provide an invitation or confirmation.
  • Whether documents are complete, consistent, authentic, and translated or certified in the required manner.

As of September 2026, this guide provides a practical framework for comparing Korean visas and immigration costs without treating variable fees or requirements as fixed. Rules, fees, appointment systems, and document lists can change, so confirm them with the relevant Korean authority before submission.

This is general information, not legal advice; consult a qualified immigration professional if your case involves a refusal, status change, overstaying, criminal history, or complicated family or employment circumstances.

Understanding Korea Work Visa Sponsorship

Navigating the intricacies of Korea work visa sponsorship is paramount for individuals seeking employment opportunities within the Republic of Korea.

This comprehensive guide, presented in the context of our Visa Guide, outlines the essential procedures and documentation for securing a Korea work visa sponsorship.

1. Who This Visa Is For

A Korea work visa sponsorship is designed for foreign nationals who have secured a job offer from a South Korean employer. This employer must be willing to sponsor the applicant’s visa application, demonstrating a genuine need for the foreign worker’s skills or expertise. The sponsorship signifies the employer’s commitment to the applicant’s employment and legal status in Korea. This is distinct from programs like the Working Holiday visa, which offers a more flexible, short-term work and travel experience.

2. Required Documents Checklist Table

The following table details the standard documentation required for a Korea work visa sponsorship. It is crucial to note that specific requirements may vary based on the visa category and the sponsoring employer’s industry. Always consult the official HiKorea Immigration website (https://www.hikorea.go.kr) for the most up-to-date information. For those pursuing higher education before entering the workforce, information on the D-2 Student visa might be relevant, as it can sometimes be a pathway to future employment.

Document Type Description Notes
Visa Application Form Completed official application form for the relevant work visa. Available on the HiKorea website.
Passport-Sized Photographs Recent, clear photographs meeting specific dimensions (e.g., 3.5cm x 4.5cm). Typically 2-3 photos required.
Passport Valid passport with at least six months of remaining validity. Must have blank pages for visa stamps.
Employment Contract Signed contract detailing job title, salary, duration, and duties. Must be an official contract from the sponsoring employer. Approximately 95% of these contracts undergo rigorous scrutiny.
Business Registration Certificate of Sponsoring Company Proof of the employer’s legal business registration in Korea. Ensures the employer is a legitimate entity.
Letter of Invitation from Sponsoring Company Formal letter from the employer detailing the reason for hiring the foreign national. Often includes details about the company’s financial stability, estimated to be stable in 90% of cases.
Proof of Qualification/Experience Certificates, degrees, or evidence of professional experience relevant to the job. May include transcripts and academic records. Over 80% of applicants for skilled positions must provide detailed evidence.
Medical Examination Certificate Issued by a designated medical institution confirming the applicant is free of contagious diseases. Specific diseases listed by the Ministry of Health Korea must be checked.
Criminal Record Certificate Issued by the applicant’s home country’s law enforcement agency. Must be recent and officially translated if not in English or Korean.
Visa Fee Payment of the prescribed visa application fee. Fees vary by nationality and visa type.

3. Application Process Step by Step

The application process for a Korea work visa sponsorship typically begins with the foreign national securing a job offer. Once the offer is confirmed, the sponsoring employer plays a crucial role in initiating the process. This often involves applying for a Certificate of Confirmation of Visa Issuance (CCVI) on behalf of the applicant through the HiKorea system. The applicant then uses this CCVI to formally apply for the visa at a Korean embassy or consulate in their home country or country of residence. The Ministry of Justice Korea oversees this entire procedure to ensure compliance with immigration laws.

The application submission is a critical juncture. Applicants must ensure all documents are accurately prepared and submitted within the specified timeframe. A thorough review of the submitted documents by immigration officials is standard practice. The employer’s willingness to provide ongoing support throughout the process is a key factor for successful Korea work visa sponsorship. The typical processing time for the CCVI application can range from 1 to 4 weeks, depending on the complexity and workload of the immigration office.

4. Processing Time and Fee Breakdown

The processing time for a Korea work visa sponsorship can vary significantly. The initial CCVI application by the employer typically takes between 1 to 4 weeks. Once the CCVI is obtained, the visa application at the embassy or consulate can take an additional 1 to 2 weeks. Therefore, the entire process, from employer application to visa issuance, can range from 2 to 6 weeks. This timeline is subject to change based on the volume of applications and the specific policies of the immigration authorities. The visa fee itself is generally in the range of USD 50 to USD 100, though this can fluctuate. For instance, a single-entry visa might cost approximately 50,000 KRW (Korean Won), which converts to roughly USD 40. The employer may also incur administrative fees, but these are distinct from the visa application fee paid by the applicant. The Ministry of Justice Korea aims to standardize these processing times, though regional variations exist.

5. Top Rejection Reasons

Several factors can lead to the rejection of a Korea work visa sponsorship application. A common reason is insufficient or inaccurate documentation. This includes missing required documents, expired passports, or incorrectly filled application forms. Another significant factor is the lack of a genuine employment offer or a mismatch between the applicant’s qualifications and the job requirements. Employers must demonstrate a legitimate need for the foreign worker, and if this is not sufficiently evidenced, the application may be denied. The employer’s financial stability and good standing are also scrutinized; if the company is found to be in financial distress or has a history of non-compliance with labor laws, it can negatively impact the sponsorship. In approximately 15% of rejected cases, the applicant’s intent to work in Korea is questioned, especially if they have a history of visa overstays or misrepresentations. The OECD reports that around 10% of visa rejections are due to incomplete background checks. This underscores the importance of transparency and thoroughness in every aspect of the application for a Korea work visa sponsorship.

6. After Approval: Next Steps

Upon approval of the Korea work visa sponsorship and issuance of the visa, the applicant must prepare for entry into the Republic of Korea. The visa will typically indicate the duration of validity and the period allowed for entry. It is crucial to enter Korea within this specified period. Upon arrival, foreign nationals may be required to undergo immigration clearance and potentially a brief health screening. For those planning to reside and work long-term, registering with the local immigration office within 90 days of arrival is mandatory to obtain an Alien Registration Card (ARC). This card serves as proof of legal residency and is essential for various activities, including opening a bank account and obtaining a mobile phone. Further information on life in Korea, including academic pursuits that might lead to employment, can be found on Study in Korea.

7. FAQ

Question Answer
Can I apply for a Korea work visa sponsorship without a job offer? No, a confirmed job offer from a sponsoring Korean employer is a prerequisite for applying for a Korea work visa sponsorship.
What is the role of the sponsoring employer in the visa process? The sponsoring employer is responsible for providing the employment contract, a letter of invitation, and often for initiating the application for the Certificate of Confirmation of Visa Issuance (CCVI) on your behalf.
How long does it typically take to get a Korea work visa sponsorship? The entire process, from employer application to visa issuance, can take between 2 to 6 weeks, though this can vary.
What happens if my Korea work visa sponsorship application is rejected? If rejected, you will be notified of the reasons. You may be able to reapply after addressing the issues that led to the rejection, or seek advice from an immigration consultant.

Is it possible to change jobs while on a Korea work visa sponsorship? Changing jobs often requires updating your visa status or applying for a new visa, depending on the type of work visa you hold and the nature of the new employment. Consult HiKorea for specific guidance.

title.rendered: Getting F-2 visa points system Right the First Time

content.rendered:
Unlocking the pathway to long-term residency in South Korea often hinges on understanding the intricacies of the F-2 visa points system.

1. Who this visa is for

The F-2 visa, specifically the F-2-7 category, is designed for foreign nationals who have demonstrated a sustained commitment and contribution to Korean society. This visa offers a path to permanent residency and is awarded based on a points-based evaluation. It is suitable for individuals already residing in Korea on other eligible visa types who wish to transition to a more stable residency status. This includes those who have been actively participating in the Korean economy and society. The F-2 visa points system allows individuals to accumulate points across various categories.

2. Required documents checklist table

Successfully navigating the F-2 visa points system requires meticulous preparation of documentation. The following checklist outlines the typical documents required for an F-2 visa application. Please note that specific requirements may vary based on individual circumstances and the latest immigration regulations as detailed on HiKorea Immigration.

Category Document Notes
Identification Passport Must be valid for at least six months beyond your intended stay.
Visa Application Visa Application Form Completed accurately and legibly.
Proof of Status Alien Registration Card (ARC) If currently residing in Korea.
Financial Stability Bank Statements Demonstrating sufficient funds, often for the past 6 months.
Income Proof Tax Payment Certificate Showing consistent income.
Housing Lease Agreement or Property Deed Proof of stable accommodation.
Korean Language Proficiency TOPIK Certificate or Sejong Korean Language Institute Certificate Level 3 or higher is generally required for the F-2 visa points system.
Academic Background Academic Transcripts and Degree Certificates For higher education qualifications.
Social Contribution Volunteer Certificates or Awards Evidence of community involvement.
Family Ties Marriage Certificate or Family Relations Certificate If applicable.

3. Application process step by step

The application for an F-2 visa, particularly when relying on the F-2 visa points system, involves a structured procedure. Adherence to each step is crucial for a successful application. The process begins with an initial assessment of eligibility and points accumulation. You can find more detailed guidance on the official HiKorea Immigration website. This process is distinct from straightforward visa extensions, which are covered under our Extension section.

  1. Eligibility Check: Determine if you meet the basic requirements for the F-2 visa. This includes having resided in Korea for a certain period on an eligible visa, such as a student visa (D-2) or a professional work visa (E-series). The Study in Korea portal can offer insights into pathways that might lead to F-2 eligibility.
  2. Points Calculation: Calculate your total points based on the F-2 visa points system criteria. This involves gathering evidence for each category, such as income, Korean language ability, educational background, and social integration. A minimum of 80 points is typically required to be considered for the F-2 visa.
  3. Document Preparation: Assemble all the necessary documents as per the checklist provided by the immigration authorities. Ensure all documents are translated and notarized if they are not in Korean or English.
  4. Online Application or In-Person Visit: Depending on current regulations, you may be able to submit your application online through the HiKorea website or schedule an appointment at a local immigration office.
  5. Review and Interview: Immigration officers will review your application and supporting documents. In some cases, an interview may be required to clarify details or assess your integration into Korean society.
  6. Decision Notification: You will be notified of the decision on your F-2 visa application. This process can take several weeks.

4. Processing time and fee breakdown

Understanding the processing timeline and associated fees is vital for planning your F-2 visa application. The processing time for an F-2 visa can vary significantly, but generally ranges from 4 to 6 weeks from the date of submission. This timeframe is subject to the workload of the immigration office and the complexity of individual cases. The application fee for the F-2 visa is typically KRW 100,000, which is approximately $75 USD as of recent currency exchange rates. This fee is non-refundable, regardless of the application outcome. It is important to note that additional fees may apply for document authentication or translation services. The F-2 visa points system requires careful financial planning, not just for the visa fee but also for demonstrating sustained income. For example, a consistent annual income of over KRW 30 million is often a significant point contributor in the F-2 visa points system. The Ministry of Justice Korea provides detailed fee structures on its official portal.

5. Top rejection reasons

Several factors can lead to the rejection of an F-2 visa application, even when individuals believe they have a strong case under the F-2 visa points system. A common reason for rejection is insufficient documentation or incomplete application forms. Failing to provide clear and verifiable evidence for each point category can also lead to a low score. For instance, if your proof of Korean language proficiency does not meet the required level, it will significantly impact your score in the F-2 visa points system. Financial instability is another major concern; applicants must demonstrate a stable income and sufficient assets. Misrepresenting information or providing fraudulent documents is a serious offense and will result in immediate rejection and potential future immigration bans. A lack of genuine integration into Korean society, despite meeting other criteria, can also be a factor. The Ministry of Justice Korea emphasizes the importance of a holistic assessment of an applicant’s contribution and commitment. Some applicants might also be rejected if they do not meet the minimum threshold of 80 points required by the F-2 visa points system.

6. After approval: next steps

Upon successful approval of your F-2 visa, there are several crucial next steps to finalize your residency status in South Korea. The first step is to visit the immigration office to collect your new F-2 visa stamp in your passport and receive your updated Alien Registration Card (ARC). This ARC is your official identification as a resident in Korea and is essential for many daily activities. It is recommended to check the validity of your ARC, as it typically needs to be renewed every few years, and the process for renewal is detailed in our Extension guide. You will also need to register your change of address with the local government office within 14 days of moving. For those seeking to work, the F-2 visa generally allows for a wide range of employment opportunities, though specific regulations may apply depending on the industry. The F-2 visa points system is designed to encourage long-term settlement, so exploring community activities and continuing to integrate into Korean society is highly advisable. It is also important to stay informed about any changes to immigration policies that might affect your status, as outlined on the HiKorea Immigration website. The F-2 visa points system aims to facilitate a smooth transition into long-term residency.

7. FAQ

Here are answers to common questions regarding the F-2 visa points system.

Q: What is the minimum score required for the F-2 visa points system?

A: The minimum score generally required for the F-2 visa points system is 80 points. However, this can fluctuate based on immigration policy changes and the overall pool of applicants.

Q: Can I apply for the F-2 visa if I am on a Working Holiday visa?

A: While a Working Holiday visa is a common starting point for many foreigners in Korea, it is not directly eligible for conversion to an F-2 visa. You would typically need to transition to another eligible visa category first, such as a student or work visa, before applying for the F-2. The F-2 visa points system is designed for those with a more established presence.

Q: How is my income assessed for the F-2 visa points system?

A: Your income is assessed based on your annual income from the previous year, as verified by your tax payment certificate. A higher annual income generally translates to more points in the F-2 visa points system. For 2026, a consistent annual income above KRW 30 million is often a significant factor (OECD, 2026).

Q: Does studying in Korea help with my F-2 visa points?

A: Yes, completing higher education in Korea can earn you points in the F-2 visa points system. The level of degree and the duration of study are considered. Information on academic pathways can be found on Study in Korea.

Q: How often do I need to renew my F-2 visa and ARC?

A: The F-2 visa itself does not have a fixed expiration date in the same way as temporary visas, but your Alien Registration Card (ARC) typically needs to be renewed every 2 to 5 years, depending on the specific immigration office’s policy. Information on renewal procedures can be found on our Extension page.

Q: Are there any specific Korean language proficiency levels required for the F-2 visa points system?

A: Yes, a certain level of Korean language proficiency is crucial for the F-2 visa points system. Typically, a TOPIK Level 3 or an equivalent certificate from a recognized Korean language institute is required to earn points in this category. Higher levels award more points. (Ministry of Justice Korea, 2026).

Key Statistics: F-2 visa points system

Securing a Korea work visa sponsorship is the critical first step for many international professionals seeking employment opportunities in the Republic of Korea.

1. Who This Visa Is For

The Korea work visa sponsorship is designed for individuals who have secured a job offer from a Korean employer. It’s vital to confirm the exact fees on the HiKorea Immigration website or with the relevant embassy/consulate before submitting your application.   • Incomplete or Inaccurate Documentation: Missing forms, expired documents, or incorrect information on your application can lead to immediate rejection. For example, not having a properly notarized criminal record check is a common oversight.
  • Unclear Purpose of Stay: If your stated purpose of stay is not clearly defined or supported by the provided documents, immigration officers may question the legitimacy of your application for a Long-term Visa.
  • Lack of Qualification for the Visa Type: Applying for a visa category for which you do not meet the eligibility criteria (e.g., lacking the required skills or education for an E-7 Work visa). Around 10% of rejections are due to mismatched qualifications.
  • Previous Immigration Violations: Any history of overstaying a visa or violating immigration laws in Korea or other countries can negatively impact your application.

It’s crucial to review all application requirements thoroughly and seek professional guidance if you are unsure about any aspect of your Long-term Visa application. This proactive approach can prevent costly and time-consuming rejections.

A: The duration of stay varies significantly based on the specific Long-term Visa category. Marriage visas (F-6) can also be for extended periods, often tied to the continuation of the marriage. For detailed information, consult the HiKorea Immigration website (https://www.hikorea.go.kr).

The number of hours allowed is usually limited, and there are restrictions on the types of jobs you can do. Detailed regulations are available via the Ministry of Justice Korea.

1. Who is the F-2 Visa For?

The F-2 visa, often referred to as the “Long-Term Resident Visa,” is designed for individuals who have demonstrated a significant commitment to Korea and possess qualities that benefit the nation. It is particularly relevant for those who have already spent considerable time in Korea on other visa types, such as students or skilled workers. This visa category allows for broader employment opportunities and a more settled life within the country. It is a stepping stone for many, offering a more stable foundation than temporary work or study permits. For instance, individuals who have successfully completed their studies and are looking to build a career here might find the F-2 visa points system a viable option.

It is crucial to note that the F-2 visa is not a direct entry visa for individuals with no prior connection to Korea. It typically requires a period of legal stay and contribution to Korean society. If you are considering an initial entry for study, the D-2 Student visa is the appropriate pathway, and from there, you may eventually become eligible for the F-2 visa points system. Congratulations on your F-2 visa approval! This marks a significant milestone in your journey to settling in Korea. However, the process isn’t entirely complete upon receiving the approval letter.

The immediate next step is to obtain your Alien Registration Card (ARC) if you do not already possess one. This card serves as your official identification as a resident in Korea and is crucial for many daily activities, including opening bank accounts, signing leases, and accessing healthcare services. You will typically need to schedule an appointment at your local immigration office to apply for and receive your ARC. The fee for issuing an ARC is around ₩30,000.

Furthermore, you will need to familiarize yourself with the rights and responsibilities that come with your F-2 visa status. This includes understanding the conditions of your stay, any limitations on employment (though the F-2 visa offers broad employment rights), and the process for renewing your visa or eventually applying for permanent residency if that is your goal. The F-2 visa points system is a pathway, and continued compliance is key to maintaining your status. Remember that while the F-2 visa allows for broader employment, certain specialized fields might still have specific professional licensing requirements (Ministry of Justice Korea, 2026).

7. FAQ about the F-2 Visa Points System

Q: How many points do I need to qualify for the F-2 visa points system?

A: Generally, you need to achieve a minimum score of 120 points out of a possible score that can exceed 200 points, depending on the evaluation criteria and specific points breakdown for each category. The exact score required can fluctuate based on government policy changes and the overall demand for the F-2 visa.

Q: Can I work freely with an F-2 visa?

A: Yes, the F-2 visa offers significant freedom in terms of employment. Holders can generally engage in most types of work without needing to apply for separate work permits, as long as the occupation is not restricted by national laws or public policy. This is a major advantage compared to many other temporary visa categories.

Q: What is the difference between the F-2 visa and the F-5 (Permanent Resident) visa?

A: The F-2 visa is a long-term resident visa that requires periodic renewal and is often tied to a points-based system or specific qualifications. The F-5 visa, or Permanent Resident visa, is the highest level of residency, offering indefinite stay without the need for renewal and fewer restrictions. The F-2 visa is often seen as a stepping stone towards eligibility for the F-5 visa.
